public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 10

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/10](https://www.erdosproblems.com/10)
- [Cr71] Crocker, R., On the sum of a prime and of two powers of two. Pacific J. Math. 36 (1971),
  103-107.
- [Ga75] Gallagher, P. X., Primes and powers of 2. Acta Arith. 29 (1976), 353-370.
- [GrSo98] Granville, A. and Soundararajan, K., A binary additive problem of Erdős and the
  order of $2$ mod $p^2$. Ramanujan J. 2 (1998), 283-298.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos10

/--
The set of natural numbers that can be written as a sum
of a prime and at most $k$ powers of $2$.
-/
abbrev sumPrimeAndTwoPows (k : ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  { p + (pows.map (2 ^ ·)).sum | (p : ℕ) (pows : Multiset ℕ) (_ : p.Prime)
    (_ : pows.card ≤ k)}

/-- A prime is the sum of a prime and no powers of $2$. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 11]
theorem two_mem_sumPrimeAndTwoPows_zero : 2 ∈ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 0 :=
  ⟨2, 0, Nat.prime_two, by simp, by simp⟩

/-- $1$ is smaller than every prime, so it lies in no `sumPrimeAndTwoPows k`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 11]
theorem one_not_mem_sumPrimeAndTwoPows (k : ℕ) : 1 ∉ sumPrimeAndTwoPows k := by
  rintro ⟨p, pows, hp, -, h⟩
  have : 2 ≤ p := hp.two_le
  omega

/--
Is there some $k$ such that every large integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$
powers of $2$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ k, ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, n ∈ sumPrimeAndTwoPows k := by
  sorry

/--
Gallagher [Ga75] has shown that for any $ϵ > 0$ there exists $k(ϵ)$
such that the set of integers which are the sum of a prime and at most $k(ϵ)$
many powers of $2$ has lower density at least $1 - ϵ$.

Ref: Gallagher, P. X., _Primes and powers of 2_.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.gallagher (ε : ℝ)
    (hε : 0 < ε) : ∃ k, 1 - ε ≤ (sumPrimeAndTwoPows k).lowerDensity := by
  sorry

/--
Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] have conjectured that at most $3$
powers of $2$ suffice for all odd integers, and hence at most $4$ powers of $2$
suffice for all even integers.

Ref: Granville, A. and Soundararajan, K., _A Binary Additive Problem of Erdős and the Order of $2$ mod $p^2$_
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.granville_soundararajan_odd :
    {n : ℕ | Odd n ∧ 1 < n} ⊆ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3 ∧
      {n : ℕ | Even n ∧ n ≠ 0} ⊆ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 4 := by
  sorry

/--
Bogdan Grechuk has observed that `1117175146` is not the sum of a prime
and at most $3$ powers of $2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.grechuk_example :
    1117175146 ∉ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3 := by
  sorry

/--
There are infinitely many even integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.two_pows :
    Set.Infinite <| {n : ℕ | Even n} \ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 2 := by
  sorry

/--
Bogdan Grechuk has observed that $1117175146$ is not the sum of a prime and at most $3$
powers of $2$, and pointed out that parity considerations, coupled with the fact that there
are many integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$ suggest that there exist
infinitely many even integers which are not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$.

This follows from Crocker's construction [Cr71] of infinitely many odd $t \equiv 15 \pmod{16}$
which are not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$: each such $t + 1$ is even and not the
sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$.

The linked Lean formalisation is by Daryxx, see comment section.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://gist.github.com/DaryxXx/e112c74cc648b08a420b0959315cf65f/4b347897ff1811f1db1d82594c581f54b8f31b7d#file-main-lean-L2287"]
theorem erdos_10.variants.grechuk :
    Set.Infinite <| {n : ℕ | Even n} \ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3 := by
  sorry

end Erdos10

findings.description: The module docstring's bibliography entry for [Ga75] is wrong: it reads "Gallagher, P. X., Primes and powers of 2. Acta Arith. 29 (1976), 353-370." Gallagher's paper appeared in Invent. Math. 29 (1975), 125–142 (DOI 10.1007/BF01390190). Gallagher has no paper in Acta Arith. 29. The page range 353–370 belongs to Montgomery–Vaughan, "The exceptional set in Goldbach's problem", Acta Arith. 27 (1975), 353–370, so the entry looks like a conflation of two citations. None of the Lean statements is affected.

Further confirmation: Crossref DOI 10.1007/BF01390190 (Inventiones Mathematicae 29, 125-142, 1975); zbMATH 0305.10044 ("Invent. findings.description: The variant states that infinitely many EVEN integers lie outside `sumPrimeAndTwoPows 2`. The only matching text in the source is Grechuk's remark about "the fact that there are many integers not the sum of a prime and 2 powers of 2 (see [9])". Problem [9] and Crocker [Cr71], which the file also cites, are about ODD integers. That odd fact is what Grechuk's parity argument needs: an odd t ∉ S₂ gives an even t+1 ∉ S₃. The Lean's even version is true, so the `research solved` tag is right. It follows from `erdos_10.variants.grechuk` because S₂ ⊆ S₃ (checked in Lean). It is also a different and much easier fact: even exceptions are small (906, 960, 1200, …) and follow from Erdős's 1950 covering-congruence result on p + 2^k. Odd exceptions need Crocker's construction, and no odd n in [3, 2·10⁵] is outside S₂ (brute force). So the declaration does not state the source's fact, although its truth is not in question. A smaller point: the docstring says "2 powers of 2", while the Lean means "at most 2".
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/10: "...parity considerations, coupled with the fact that there are many integers not the sum of a prime and 2 powers of 2 (see [9]) suggest that there exist infinitely many even integers which are not the sum of a prime and at most 3 powers of 2". erdosproblems.com/9: "Let A be the set of all odd integers ≥1 not of the form p+2^k+2^l (where k,l≥0 and p is prime)... Crocker [Cr71] proved that there are infinitely many odd integers not of this form". Crocker, Pacific J. Math. 36 (1971) 103–107, Theorem I (msp.org/pjm/1971/36-1/p09.xhtml): "There is an infinity of distinct, positive odd integers not representable as the sum of a prime and of two positive powers of 2."
findings.suggested_fix: If the variant is meant to formalize the remark, use the odd statement (Crocker's theorem; the linked gist's `family_not_S2` already provides it): `theorem erdos_10.variants.two_pows : Set.Infinite <| {n : ℕ | Odd n} \ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 2`, with docstring "There are infinitely many odd integers not the sum of a prime and at most 2 powers of 2 [Cr71]." Otherwise keep the even version, but document it as a weaker consequence of `erdos_10.variants.grechuk`, not as the source's remark.

reformulations.difference: "At most k powers of 2" is modelled as the sum of `2^a` over a `Multiset ℕ` of exponents with card ≤ k. Exponents may repeat, and exponent 0 (the power 1 = 2^0) is allowed.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Repetition is harmless. Merging 2^a + 2^a = 2^(a+1) never increases the number of terms, so "at most k powers with repetition" = "at most k distinct powers" = "p + m with binary digit sum of m ≤ k". That is the Hamming-weight definition in OEIS A387053, which the source links. Allowing 2^0 is the source's own convention. Its "hence at most 4 powers of 2 suffice for all even integers" works only via n = (n−1) + 2^0. Without 2^0, every even n would need p = 2 and popcount(n−2) ≤ k, so the main question would be trivially negative. For odd n the variants agree whether or not 2^0 is allowed.

reformulations.difference: The Lean states a conjunction: odd n > 1 lie in S₃, and even n ≠ 0 lie in S₄. The source states a conjecture about odd integers plus its 'hence' consequence for even integers, without excluding 1 or 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The even conjunct follows from the odd one: n = 2 is prime, and for even n ≥ 4, n−1 is odd and > 1, so adding one 2^0 gives n ∈ S₄. So the conjunction is equivalent to the odd conjecture alone. I proved this `↔` in a scratch file (`gs_iff`). The integers 0 and 1 are not a prime plus a sum of powers of 2 at all (see the file's test `one_not_mem_sumPrimeAndTwoPows`), so excluding them is the only meaningful reading of "all odd/even integers".

could_not_verify: Erdos10.erdos_10.variants.granville_soundararajan_odd: I could not read the exact wording of the conjecture in [GrSo98] (Ramanujan J. 2 (1998) 283–298, paywalled; the abstract and zbMATH review don't mention it). The odd-integer statement comes out the same whether or not 2^0 or repeated powers are allowed, and no odd counterexample exists up to 2·10^6.
review.notes:
Every other declaration checks out against the source.
- `erdos_10`: its right-hand side is the source's question itself, not the negation. It is correctly tagged `research open`, and erdosproblems.com and the teorth database both record the problem as open.
- `gallagher`: the statement matches the source text exactly. Gallagher's paper states the result for odd integers (from its opening page: "the density of odd integers which may be written in the form n = p + 2^{ν1}+...+2^{νk} tends to 1 as k→∞"). The source's version for all integers, and the Lean, follow from it by n ↦ n+1 with 2^0 (k ↦ k+1).
- `grechuk_example`: I recomputed it. 1117175146 is not in S₃: no n − m is prime for any m with Hamming weight ≤ 3, checked with both a deterministic Miller–Rabin test and trial division. The number is in S₄.
- `grechuk` (research solved, formal_proof): the gist's Main.lean has SHA-256 784bb738…, the same as the proof claim. It has no imports and does not define `Erdos10.sumPrimeAndTwoPows` itself, so I compiled it on top of `FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«10»` with this repo's toolchain (Lean v4.33.1; the gist says 4.27). One step fails from simp-normal-form drift: `simpa [CrockerFixedDataPrimefree.rows, rowModulus] using CrockerExactOrdersFinal.verified_table_28`. It succeeds once replaced by `exact CrockerExactOrdersFinal.verified_table_28`. After that, `#print axioms target` gives [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], and `target` has exactly the type of `erdos_10.variants.grechuk`. The link is pinned to a revision, and L2287 is `theorem target`. So the solved status and the formal_proof record are justified, but the linked file needs this one-line patch on the current toolchain.
- Status: I found no status issues.
- OEIS A387053 carries a formula comment: "Johnston & Trudgian prove, on GRH, that a(2n) <= 6". Their paper (arXiv:2605.17825) is about the Linnik–Goldbach problem, i.e. two primes plus 6 powers of 2. So it gives no conditional resolution of Erdős 10, and `research open` stands.
- Brute-force checks: every n in [2, 2·10^6] is in S₃, so the G–S statement is consistent there. The smallest positive even number outside S₂ is 906.
- Naming only (not a math issue): `granville_soundararajan_odd` also contains the even conjunct.
